questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| Plant | Description |
|---|---|
| I. Cassava | Woody shrub |
| II. Ginger | Herb with pseudostem |
| III. Malabar spinach | Herbaceous climber |
| IV. Mint | Annual shrub |
| V. Papaya | Woody shrub |

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
Three pairs are right; mint and papaya are mislabelled.
- I. Cassava — a **woody shrub** (tapioca). ✓
- II. Ginger — a herb whose upright shoot is a **pseudostem** of rolled leaf sheaths, like banana's. ✓
- III. Malabar spinach (*Basella*) — a **herbaceous climber**. ✓
- IV. Mint — a **perennial herb**, not an annual shrub. ✗
- V. Papaya — botanically a giant soft-stemmed, **tree-like herb**; its trunk is not truly woody. ✗

Answer (b). Worth keeping: papaya and banana are giant herbs, not trees — plant **habit** (herb/shrub/climber) is a different axis from crop use, and UPSC tests the habit.
questions.tagging_note: Real gap: this is plant morphology (habit — shrub, herb, climber), and no topic covers botany. SNT-01 basic biology is cell/genetics/human systems and does not reach plant habit; GEO-17 only catches these as crops.

independent_answer.reasoning: Cassava (woody shrub), ginger (herb with pseudostem) and Malabar spinach (herbaceous climber) match; mint is a perennial herb, not an annual shrub, and papaya is a soft-stemmed giant herb, not woody — three.

questions.stem:
With reference to the planet Earth, consider the following statements :
I. Rain forests produce more oxygen than that produced by oceans.
II. Marine phytoplankton and photosynthetic bacteria produce about 50% of world's oxygen.
III. Well-oxygenated surface water contains several folds higher oxygen than that in atmospheric air.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
options: None of the above statements is correct
questions.explanation_md:
Only the phytoplankton statement stands.
- I — the oceans, not rainforests, lead oxygen production; the "Amazon makes 20% of our oxygen" line is a myth, and forests consume most of what they produce through respiration and decay. ✗
- II — marine **phytoplankton** and photosynthetic bacteria (e.g. *Prochlorococcus*) produce about **50%** of the world's oxygen. ✓
- III — inverted: well-aerated surface water holds far **less** oxygen per volume (~8–10 mg/L) than air does — which is exactly why dissolved-oxygen crashes kill fish. ✗

Answer (b). Worth keeping: the ocean supplies roughly half of Earth's oxygen, and water carries dozens of times less O2 per unit volume than air.
questions.tagging_note: Oxygen production and dissolved oxygen sit between the oxygen cycle (ENV-02) and marine ecosystems (ENV-04); neither is an exact fit.

independent_answer.reasoning: Oceans (phytoplankton/cyanobacteria) produce about half the world's oxygen — more than rainforests (I false), and water holds far less O2 per volume than air (III false), so II only.

questions.stem:
Consider the following types of vehicles :
I. Full battery electric vehicles
II. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles
III. Fuel cell-electric hybrid vehicles
How many of the above are considered as alternative powertrain vehicles?
questions.explanation_md:
An **alternative powertrain** is any propulsion system other than the conventional petrol/diesel internal combustion drivetrain — so all three listed types qualify.
- I. Full battery electric vehicles — electric motor powered solely by a battery pack; the classic alternative powertrain. **Counts.**
- II. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles — a fuel cell stack converts hydrogen to electricity on board; no combustion drivetrain. **Counts.**
- III. Fuel cell-electric hybrids — pair a fuel cell with a battery/electric motor; still no conventional ICE drivetrain. **Counts.**
Nothing here is a trick: the family also includes plug-in hybrids, strong hybrids and even CNG/flex-fuel variants in broader usage — the defining test is *departure from the pure ICE drivetrain*, not the fuel alone.
Remember: BEV, HEV, PHEV and FCEV are all "alternative powertrains"; the term is about the propulsion architecture, not just zero emissions.
questions.tagging_note: Format stretch: options are counts of listed items, not of pairs or statements. The vocabulary has no generic 'how many of the above' slug, so pairs is used as the count format.

independent_answer.reasoning: BEVs, hydrogen fuel cell vehicles and fuel cell-electric hybrids are all alternative (non-ICE) powertrain vehicles.

questions.stem:
With reference to Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), consider the following statements :
I. All types of UAVs can do vertical landing.
II. All types of UAVs can do automated hovering.
III. All types of UAVs can use battery only as a source of power supply.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Every statement generalises with "**all types**" — and fixed-wing and engine-powered UAVs break each one, so none is correct.
- I. Vertical landing — **wrong**. Fixed-wing UAVs (e.g. surveillance drones like Heron-class) land on runways or by belly/parachute recovery; only rotary-wing and VTOL designs land vertically.
- II. Automated hovering — **wrong**. Hovering needs rotor-borne lift; a fixed-wing UAV stalls below its minimum airspeed and cannot hover at all.
- III. Battery-only power — **wrong**. Many UAVs run on petrol/diesel piston engines, turboprops, hydrogen fuel cells or solar-electric hybrids; batteries dominate only small multirotors.
UPSC's favourite trap in tech questions is the absolute quantifier: "all types can" fails if a single class of UAV cannot. Fixed-wing drones are the standing counterexample to hover/vertical-landing claims.

independent_answer.reasoning: Fixed-wing UAVs can neither land vertically nor hover, and many UAVs use combustion engines, so no statement holds for all types.

questions.stem:
In the context of electric vehicle batteries, consider the following elements :
I. Cobalt
II. Graphite
III. Lithium
IV. Nickel
How many of the above usually make up battery cathodes?
questions.explanation_md:
Lithium, cobalt and nickel sit in the **cathode**; graphite is the standard **anode** material — so only three of the four make up cathodes.
- I. Cobalt — **cathode**. Part of NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) and NCA chemistries; stabilises the layered oxide structure.
- II. Graphite — **not cathode**. It is the dominant anode, hosting lithium ions during charging.
- III. Lithium — **cathode**. The cathode is a lithium metal oxide/phosphate (LiNiMnCoO₂, LiFePO₄); lithium ions shuttle between electrodes.
- IV. Nickel — **cathode**. High-nickel cathodes raise energy density; the push to cut cobalt raises nickel content.
Durable split to memorise: **cathode = Li + Ni + Co + Mn (or Fe-P in LFP); anode = graphite (moving toward silicon)**. That one line answers most EV-battery-materials questions, including why cobalt and nickel dominate critical-minerals diplomacy.
questions.tagging_note: Format stretch: counts listed elements, not pairs or statements; pairs used as the count format for want of a 'how many of the above' slug.

independent_answer.reasoning: Lithium, cobalt and nickel are cathode constituents; graphite is the anode material.

questions.stem:
Consider the following :
I. Cigarette butts
II. Eyeglass lenses
III. Car tyres
How many of them contain plastic?
questions.explanation_md:
All three contain plastic — each is a well-documented, non-obvious source of plastic and microplastic pollution.
- I. Cigarette butts — **plastic**. Filters are made of **cellulose acetate**, a plastic fibre; butts are among the most littered plastic items on Earth.
- II. Eyeglass lenses — **plastic**. Modern lenses are overwhelmingly polycarbonate or CR-39 resin, not glass.
- III. Car tyres — **plastic**. Tyres are largely synthetic rubber (styrene-butadiene and similar polymers); road abrasion of tyres is one of the biggest single sources of environmental microplastics.
The question rewards knowing that "plastic" means synthetic/semi-synthetic polymers generally — not just packaging. Cellulose acetate filters and synthetic-rubber tyre wear are the two examples worth banking for any microplastics question.
questions.tagging_note: Format stretch: counts listed objects, not pairs or statements; pairs used as the count format.

independent_answer.reasoning: Cigarette filters (cellulose acetate), eyeglass lenses (polycarbonate/CR-39) and tyres (synthetic rubber polymers) all contain plastic.

questions.stem:
Consider the following substances :
I. Ethanol
II. Nitroglycerine
III. Urea
Coal gasification technology can be used in the production of how many of them?
questions.explanation_md:
Coal gasification yields **syngas (CO + H₂)**, which feeds ammonia–urea and methanol–ethanol chains — but nitroglycerine is made by a nitration route that gasification does not serve.
- I. Ethanol — **yes**. Syngas can be converted to ethanol via catalytic routes (through methanol/DME) or syngas fermentation; coal-to-ethanol plants exist.
- II. Nitroglycerine — **no**. It is produced by nitrating glycerol with concentrated nitric–sulphuric acid; glycerol comes from fats/oils or propylene, not from syngas.
- III. Urea — **yes**. Hydrogen from syngas makes ammonia, and ammonia + CO₂ makes urea. India's **Talcher Fertilizers** plant is built precisely on coal-gasification-to-urea.
So two of the three.
Remember the chain: **coal → syngas (CO + H₂) → ammonia/urea, methanol, ethanol, SNG** — with Talcher as the flagship Indian example under the National Coal Gasification Mission.
questions.tagging_note: Two problems: format counts listed substances rather than pairs/statements, and coal gasification chemistry has no real home — SNT-12 is batteries/EV/hydrogen/solar and ENV-16 is renewables only, so coal-to-chemicals falls through the tree.

independent_answer.reasoning: Coal-gasification syngas yields ethanol, ammonia-derived urea, and nitric acid used to make nitroglycerine, so all three.

questions.review_flag: Official key says b, independent reasoning said c.

questions.stem: What is the common characteristic of the chemical substances generally known as CL-20, HMX and LLM-105, which are sometimes talked about in media?
options: These are alternatives to hydrofluorocarbon refrigerants
These are explosives in military weapons
These are high-energy fuels for cruise missiles
These are fuels for rocket propulsion
questions.explanation_md:
CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are all **high-energy explosive compounds** used in military munitions — CL-20 (hexanitrohexaazaisowurtzitane) is among the most powerful non-nuclear explosives known, HMX (octogen) is a standard high explosive in warheads, and LLM-105 is an insensitive high explosive valued for safety in handling.
- (a) wrong — refrigerant alternatives to HFCs are things like HFOs, ammonia and CO₂, chemically unrelated to nitramine explosives.
- (c) and (d) wrong — these are **explosives, not fuels**: cruise missiles fly on jet fuel and rockets on propellants (HTPB, kerosene-LOX, hydrazine); explosives detonate in the warhead, they do not provide sustained propulsion.
The distinction that generalises: **propellant/fuel burns controllably for thrust; an explosive detonates for blast** — UPSC often hides the answer in that difference. India-link: these energetic materials appear in news around DRDO's advanced warhead formulations.

independent_answer.reasoning: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high-energy military explosives, not propellant fuels.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. It is expected that Majorana 1 chip will enable quantum computing.
II. Majorana 1 chip has been introduced by Amazon Web Services (AWS).
III. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Majorana 1 is **Microsoft's** topological quantum computing chip, so the AWS attribution in II is the single planted error.
- I. **Correct.** Majorana 1 (unveiled February 2025) uses topological qubits based on Majorana particles and is expected to enable scalable, error-resistant quantum computing.
- II. **Wrong.** It was introduced by **Microsoft**, not Amazon Web Services. (AWS's own 2025 quantum chip was named Ocelot — a likely inspiration for this distractor.)
- III. **Correct.** Deep learning is a subset of machine learning (neural networks with many layers), which in turn is a subset of AI — the standard nesting.
Hence I and III only.
Bank the attribution table for current-affairs tech: **Majorana 1 → Microsoft; Willow → Google; Ocelot → AWS** — company–chip mismatches are an easy mark for question-setters.

independent_answer.reasoning: Majorana 1 is Microsoft's quantum chip (not AWS), and deep learning is indeed a subset of machine learning, so I and III.

questions.stem:
With reference to monoclonal antibodies, often mentioned in news, consider the following statements :
I. They are man-made proteins.
II. They stimulate immunological function due to their ability to bind to specific antigens.
III. They are used in treating viral infections like that of Nipah virus.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
All three statements are textbook-true of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs): lab-made proteins engineered to bind one specific antigen, with proven antiviral uses.
- I. **Correct.** mAbs are man-made in the sense that they are produced in the laboratory from cloned immune cells (classically hybridoma technology); chemically they are proteins (immunoglobulins).
- II. **Correct.** Each mAb binds a single specific antigen/epitope; that binding can neutralise a pathogen directly or flag it for immune attack, thereby engaging immunological function.
- III. **Correct.** mAbs are used against viral infections — the **m102.4** monoclonal antibody has been given for **Nipah** exposure (India sourced it during the Kerala outbreaks), and mAbs were widely used against COVID-19 and Ebola.
Durable line: monoclonal = one parent cell clone, one antigen target — which is exactly why they work as precision drugs in cancer, autoimmune disease and viral outbreaks.

independent_answer.reasoning: Monoclonal antibodies are lab-made proteins that bind specific antigens and have been used against Nipah virus.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. No virus can survive in ocean waters.
II. No virus can infect bacteria.
III. No virus can change the cellular transcriptional activity in host cells.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Each statement is an absolute "**no virus can...**" claim, and each has famous counterexamples — so none is correct.
- I. **Wrong.** Oceans are the planet's largest viral reservoir — marine viruses are the most abundant biological entities in seawater and drive nutrient cycling by lysing plankton and bacteria.
- II. **Wrong.** **Bacteriophages** are viruses that infect bacteria — the basis of phage therapy against antibiotic-resistant infections.
- III. **Wrong.** Reprogramming host transcription is central to how viruses work: they hijack the host's transcriptional machinery to make viral proteins (HIV integrating into the genome is the extreme case).
So the count is zero.
The reusable lesson: in biology, a statement beginning "no organism/virus can" is almost always false — life's diversity supplies a counterexample, and bacteriophages are the counterexample UPSC reaches for most.
questions.tagging_note: Counting format on statements, not pairs. Pure virology (bacteriophages, marine viruses, host transcription) has no dedicated topic; SNT-01 basic biology is the nearest fit.

independent_answer.reasoning: Marine viruses abound, bacteriophages infect bacteria, and viruses alter host transcription, so all three statements are false.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I :
Activated carbon is a good and an attractive tool to remove pollutants from effluent streams and to remediate contaminants from various industries.
Statement II :
Activated carbon exhibits a large surface area and a strong potential for adsorbing heavy metals.
Statement III :
Activated carbon can be easily synthesized from environmental wastes with high carbon content.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement II and Statement III are correct and both of them explain Statement I
Both Statement II and Statement III are correct but only one of them explains Statement I
Only one of the Statements II and III is correct and that explains Statement I
Neither Statement II nor Statement III is correct
questions.explanation_md:
Both supporting statements are true, and each independently explains why activated carbon is a "**good and attractive**" remediation tool — II explains why it works, III explains why it is cheap and attractive.
- Statement I — **correct**. Activated carbon is a standard adsorbent for treating industrial effluents and contaminated streams.
- Statement II — **correct, explains I**. Its enormous internal surface area (hundreds to >1000 m²/g from its porous structure) gives it strong adsorption capacity for heavy metals and organic pollutants — the mechanism behind its effectiveness.
- Statement III — **correct, explains I**. It can be synthesised from high-carbon wastes (coconut shell, rice husk, sawdust), which makes it low-cost and sustainable — the reason it is *attractive*, not merely good.
Since both are correct and both explain I, (a) fits.
Remember the mechanism word: **adsorption** (surface binding), not absorption — surface area is the whole game in activated carbon, zeolites and MOF-type materials.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles ENV pollution remediation and SNT new materials (adsorption, surface area).

independent_answer.reasoning: Both II (adsorptive capacity makes it good) and III (cheap synthesis from waste makes it attractive) are correct and each explains Statement I.

questions.stem:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. An Ordinance can amend any Central Act.
II. An Ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right.
III. An Ordinance can come into effect from a back date.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
An ordinance under **Article 123** has the same force — and the same limits — as an Act of Parliament: it can do whatever Parliament can by law (amend Acts, operate retrospectively) but cannot do what Parliament cannot (violate Fundamental Rights).
- I. **Correct.** Since an ordinance is co-extensive with Parliament's legislative power, it can amend any Central Act.
- II. **Wrong.** An ordinance is "law" under **Article 13**, so one abridging a Fundamental Right would be void to that extent — exactly like an unconstitutional statute.
- III. **Correct.** Like legislation, an ordinance can be given retrospective effect from a back date.
Hence I and III only.
The generalising principle (from *A.K. Roy* and *D.C. Wadhwa*): ordinance-making is legislative power exercised by the executive — same reach, same constitutional limitations, plus the extra sunset of ceasing six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.
questions.tagging_note: Ordinance power sits in POL-17 (President/Governor); statement II is an Art 13 point from POL-07.

independent_answer.reasoning: An ordinance can amend Central Acts and operate retrospectively, but being 'law' under Art 13 it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| State | Description |
|---|---|
| I. Arunachal Pradesh | The capital is named after a fort, and the State has two National Parks |
| II. Nagaland | The State came into existence on the basis of a Constitutional Amendment Act |
| III. Tripura | Initially a Part 'C' State, it became a centrally administered territory with the reorganization of States in 1956 and later attained the status of a full-fledged State |

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
All three descriptions are accurate pieces of North-East static GK.
- I. Arunachal Pradesh — **correct**. Capital **Itanagar** takes its name from the historic **Ita Fort**, and the state has two National Parks: **Namdapha** and **Mouling**.
- II. Nagaland — **correct**. Nagaland's creation was effected through the **13th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962** (which also inserted the special provision Article 371A); it became a state in 1963.
- III. Tripura — **correct**. The princely state merged with India in 1949 and became a **Part C state**; the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 made it a centrally administered **Union Territory**; full statehood came in **1972** under the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971.
So all three pairs match.
Worth banking: 1972 was the big NE year — Tripura, Manipur and Meghalaya all became full states together; Nagaland (1963) and Arunachal/Mizoram (1987) bracket it.
questions.tagging_note: Straddles subjects: state formation/reorganisation (POL-05) plus a national-parks count (ENV-06) and capital-city static GK that no topic squarely covers.

independent_answer.reasoning: Arunachal (Itanagar/Ita Fort, Namdapha and Mouling NPs) and Tripura are correct, but Nagaland was created by the State of Nagaland Act 1962, an ordinary law, not a Constitutional Amendment.

questions.review_flag: Official key says c, independent reasoning said b.

questions.stem:
With reference to India, consider the following :
I. The Inter-State Council
II. The National Security Council
III. Zonal Councils
How many of the above were established as per the provisions of the Constitution of India?
questions.explanation_md:
Only the Inter-State Council flows from the Constitution's own text; the other two were created outside it.
- I. Inter-State Council — **constitutional**. **Article 263** empowers the President to establish it, and it was actually set up by presidential order in **1990** on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation.
- II. National Security Council — **not constitutional**. A purely executive body created in **1998**; it is neither constitutional nor statutory.
- III. Zonal Councils — **not constitutional**. They are **statutory**, created by the **States Reorganisation Act, 1956** (the North Eastern Council by its own Act of 1971) — a favourite UPSC confusion with the constitutional Inter-State Council.
So only one.
The three-way classification worth internalising: **constitutional** (in the Constitution's text), **statutory** (by an Act of Parliament), **executive** (by government resolution) — most "body" questions are just this sorting exercise.

independent_answer.reasoning: Only the Inter-State Council (Art 263) is constitutional; NSC is an executive body and Zonal Councils are statutory under the States Reorganisation Act 1956.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
I. The Constitution of India explicitly mentions that in certain spheres the Governor of a State acts in his/her own discretion.
II. The President of India can, of his/her own, reserve a bill passed by a State Legislature for his/her consideration without it being forwarded by the Governor of the State concerned.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
The Governor — unlike the President — has **explicitly mentioned discretionary powers**, while reservation of state bills is exclusively the Governor's gateway, so I stands and II falls.
- I. **Correct.** **Article 163** itself contemplates functions the Governor exercises "in his discretion," and specific provisions confer such discretion — e.g. Article 371A (Nagaland), the Sixth Schedule role for tribal areas, and reserving bills under Article 200. The President's constitution contains no parallel express discretion.
- II. **Wrong.** Under **Articles 200–201**, a bill reaches the President only when the **Governor reserves it**; the President has no power to reach out and pull a state bill for consideration on his own motion.
The durable contrast: President — aid and advice binding (Article 74, post-42nd/44th Amendments), no express discretion; Governor — aid and advice *except* where the Constitution requires discretion, and that discretion is textually acknowledged in Article 163.

independent_answer.reasoning: Art 163 explicitly mentions the Governor's discretion, but only the Governor (Art 200) can reserve a state bill for the President.

questions.stem:
Consider the following pairs :

| Provision in the Constitution of India | Stated under |
|---|---|
| I. Separation of Judiciary from the Executive in the public services of the State | The Directive Principles of the State Policy |
| II. Valuing and preserving of the rich heritage of our composite culture | The Fundamental Duties |
| III. Prohibition of employment of children below the age of 14 years in factories | The Fundamental Rights |

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
All three provisions are matched to their correct chapter of the Constitution.
- I. Separation of judiciary from executive in the public services of the State — **correct**: **Article 50**, a Directive Principle of State Policy.
- II. Valuing and preserving the rich heritage of our composite culture — **correct**: **Article 51A(f)**, a Fundamental Duty (the near-identical DPSP phrase in Article 49 is about monuments, a standard confusion).
- III. Prohibition of employment of children below 14 in factories — **correct**: **Article 24**, a Fundamental Right under the right against exploitation.
All three pairs match.
The pattern to remember: several themes recur across FR/DPSP/FD with slightly different wording (children — Articles 24, 39(e)-(f), 45, 51A(k); culture — Articles 29, 49, 51A(f)); the question is always *which chapter this exact phrasing sits in*, and "composite culture" is the signature phrase of 51A(f).
questions.tagging_note: Deliberately spans three chapters: Art 50 (DPSP), Art 51A(f) (Fundamental Duties), Art 24 (Fundamental Rights).

independent_answer.reasoning: Art 50 is a DPSP, Art 51A(f) a Fundamental Duty, and Art 24 a Fundamental Right, so all three pairs match.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
With reference to the Constitution of India, if an area in a State is declared as Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule
I. the State Government loses its executive power in such areas and a local body assumes total administration
II. the Union Government can take over the total administration of such areas under certain circumstances on the recommendations of the Governor
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Declaring a Fifth Schedule Scheduled Area changes how the State governs — it does not displace the State government, and the Centre's role is to give **directions**, not take over.
- I. **Wrong.** The executive power of the State expressly **extends to its Scheduled Areas**. The Governor gains special functions (reports to the President, power to adapt or bar laws) and a **Tribes Advisory Council** advises — but no local body assumes total administration.
- II. **Wrong.** Para 3 of the Fifth Schedule lets the Union give **directions to the State** regarding administration of Scheduled Areas; nothing allows the Union to take over total administration on the Governor's recommendation.
Hence neither.
The clean contrast to carry: **Fifth Schedule** — State administers, Governor reports, Centre directs; **Sixth Schedule** — elected Autonomous District Councils actually exercise legislative and executive powers. Statement I describes something closer to the Sixth Schedule, which is the trap.

independent_answer.reasoning: In Fifth Schedule areas the State retains executive power and the Union may only give directions, not assume total administration, so neither statement is correct.

questions.stem:
With reference to India, consider the following pairs :

| Organization | Union Ministry |
|---|---|
| I. The National Automotive Board | Ministry of Commerce and Industry |
| II. The Coir Board | Ministry of Heavy Industries |
| III. The National Centre for Trade Information | Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises |

How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
questions.explanation_md:
The three organisations have simply been rotated one ministry off their real parents — every pair is mismatched.
- I. National Automotive Board — **wrong**. It functions under the **Ministry of Heavy Industries** (it oversees the NATRiP/automotive testing infrastructure), not Commerce and Industry.
- II. Coir Board — **wrong**. A statutory board under the **Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises** (like the KVIC), not Heavy Industries.
- III. National Centre for Trade Information — **wrong**. Set up by ITPO and NIC, it comes under the **Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, not MSME.
So none is correctly matched — each description actually belongs to one of the other rows.
The test-taking lesson: when every entry in a matching table looks plausible, check for a **cyclic shuffle** — UPSC's cheapest way to build an "all wrong" key from true ministry names.
questions.tagging_note: Gap in the syllabus tree: no topic covers static GK mapping of boards/bodies to their parent Union ministry. ECO-15 (industry/MSME) is only an approximate home for Coir Board and the National Automotive Board.

independent_answer.reasoning: National Automotive Board is under Heavy Industries, Coir Board under MSME, and NCTI under Commerce and Industry, so all three pairs are mismatched.

questions.stem:
Consider the following subjects under the Constitution of India :
I. List I–Union List, in the Seventh Schedule
II. Extent of the executive power of a State
III. Conditions of the Governor's office
For a constitutional amendment with respect to which of the above, ratification by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States is required before presenting the bill to the President of India for assent?
questions.explanation_md:
The proviso to **Article 368(2)** lists the federal provisions needing ratification by half the State legislatures — Seventh Schedule lists and executive power are on it; the Governor's service conditions are not.
- I. Union List, Seventh Schedule — **needs ratification**. Any change to the Seventh Schedule lists redistributes Union–State legislative power, squarely in the proviso.
- II. Extent of the executive power of a State — **needs ratification**. Articles 73 and 162 (extent of Union and State executive power) are expressly listed.
- III. Conditions of the Governor's office — **no ratification**. Governor provisions (Articles 153–162 generally) are amendable by Parliament's **special majority alone**.
Hence I and II only.
Memorise the proviso's family: election of the President (Arts 54, 55), extent of executive power (73, 162), Union judiciary and High Courts, legislative relations, Seventh Schedule, representation of States in Parliament, and Article 368 itself — everything else needs at most special majority.

independent_answer.reasoning: Amendments to Seventh Schedule lists and Art 162 (state executive power) need state ratification, but Governor's office conditions do not fall under the Art 368 proviso.

questions.stem:
With reference to the Indian polity, consider the following statements :
I. The Governor of a State is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his/her office.
II. No criminal proceedings shall be instituted or continued against the Governor during his/her term of office.
III. Members of a State Legislature are not liable to any proceedings in any court in respect of anything said within the House.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Statements I and II restate **Article 361** (personal immunity of the President and Governors) and III restates **Article 194** (legislative privilege) — all three are correct.
- I. **Correct.** Article 361(1): the Governor is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of the office (judicial review of the *action* remains possible; the person is immune).
- II. **Correct.** Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President or a Governor **during the term of office**; even arrest is barred (clause 3).
- III. **Correct.** Article 194(2): no member of a State Legislature is liable to proceedings in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given in the House (Article 105 is the parliamentary twin).
Durable pairing: **Art 361 — personal immunity of President/Governor (criminal absolute during term; civil needs 2 months' notice); Arts 105/194 — freedom of speech in the House**.

independent_answer.reasoning: Art 361(1) and 361(2) protect the Governor and Art 194(2) protects legislators for speech in the House, so all three are correct.

questions.stem:
Consider the following activities :
I. Production of crude oil
II. Refining, storage and distribution of petroleum
III. Marketing and sale of petroleum products
IV. Production of natural gas
How many of the above activities are regulated by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board in our country?
questions.explanation_md:
PNGRB regulates the **downstream and midstream** petroleum sector; upstream **production** of crude oil and natural gas is expressly outside its mandate — so only two of the four activities fall to it.
- I. Production of crude oil — **not PNGRB**. Exploration and production are administered through the **Directorate General of Hydrocarbons** under the petroleum ministry.
- II. Refining, storage and distribution — **PNGRB**. The PNGRB Act, 2006 covers refining, processing, storage, transportation and distribution.
- III. Marketing and sale of petroleum products — **PNGRB**. Marketing and sale are named functions, including authorising city gas distribution networks.
- IV. Production of natural gas — **not PNGRB**. Same upstream exclusion as crude oil.
Hence only two.
The one-line split to remember: **upstream (E&P) → DGH; downstream/midstream (refining to retail, pipelines, CGD) → PNGRB, under the PNGRB Act, 2006** — the Act's own title section excludes production.
questions.tagging_note: Counting format applied to activities. Tests the PNGRB's statutory mandate; no regulator-specific topic exists, so ECO-16 (energy/infrastructure) carries it.

independent_answer.reasoning: PNGRB regulates downstream refining, storage, distribution, marketing and sale, but not upstream production of crude oil or natural gas.

questions.stem:
Suppose the revenue expenditure is ₹ 80,000 crores and the revenue receipts of the Government are ₹ 60,000 crores. The Government budget also shows borrowings of ₹ 10,000 crores and interest payments of ₹ 6,000 crores. Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Revenue deficit is ₹ 20,000 crores.
II. Fiscal deficit is ₹ 10,000 crores.
III. Primary deficit is ₹ 4,000 crores.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
All three numbers drop straight out of the three deficit definitions.
- I — Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts = 80,000 − 60,000 = **₹20,000 crore**. Correct.
- II — Fiscal deficit is, by definition, the government's **total borrowing requirement**; the budget shows borrowings of ₹10,000 crore, so fiscal deficit = ₹10,000 crore. Correct.
- III — Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 10,000 − 6,000 = **₹4,000 crore**. Correct.
Worth remembering: fiscal deficit = total borrowings; primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments; revenue deficit looks only at the revenue account. Interest payments are revenue expenditure, but you never subtract them for revenue deficit — only for primary deficit.

independent_answer.reasoning: Revenue deficit = 80k-60k = 20k; fiscal deficit = borrowings = 10k; primary deficit = 10k-6k = 4k, so all three statements are correct.

questions.stem: India is one of the founding members of the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a multimodal transportation corridor, which will connect
options: India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran
India to Central Asia via China
India to South-East Asia through Bangladesh and Myanmar
questions.explanation_md:
The INSTC is a ~7,200 km multimodal route running Mumbai → Bandar Abbas (**Iran**) → Caspian Sea → Russia, with links onward to Central Asia and northern Europe — so "India to Central Asia to Europe via Iran" is the right description.
- (b) wrong — China is not on the corridor at all.
- (c) wrong — that describes the India–Myanmar–Thailand / Kaladan style eastward connectivity, not INSTC.
- (d) wrong — Azerbaijan lies on the corridor's western branch, but a description that routes India to Europe "through Azerbaijan" while omitting Iran misses the corridor's spine.
Worth remembering: founding agreement signed in **2000 at St. Petersburg by India, Iran and Russia**; INSTC is the Suez-bypassing north–south route, cutting time and cost to Russia/Europe roughly in half.

independent_answer.reasoning: INSTC (India, Iran, Russia founding members) links India via Iran to Central Asia, Russia and Europe.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
Statement I :
Of the two major ethanol producers in the world, i.e., Brazil and the United States of America, the former produces more ethanol than the latter.
Statement II :
Unlike in the United States of America where corn is the principal feedstock for ethanol production, sugarcane is the principal feedstock for ethanol production in Brazil.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II explains Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II does not explain Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is not correct
Statement I is not correct but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation_md:
Statement I inverts the ranking — the **United States is the world's largest ethanol producer** (roughly half of global output), with Brazil a clear second — while Statement II states the feedstocks correctly.
- I — incorrect: Brazil pioneered fuel ethanol but was overtaken by the US in the mid-2000s; the US now produces substantially more.
- II — correct: **corn** is the principal US feedstock; **sugarcane** is Brazil's.
So Statement I is wrong and Statement II is right — option (d).
Worth remembering for the India angle: India's E20 ethanol-blending programme leans on sugarcane and increasingly on maize/damaged grain — the same corn-vs-cane split this question tests globally.
questions.tagging_note: Biofuel feedstocks and world ethanol output straddle ENV-16 (biofuels) and GEO-23 (world economic geography); neither owns it cleanly.

independent_answer.reasoning: USA is the world's largest ethanol producer (corn-based), so Statement I is false while Statement II (sugarcane in Brazil, corn in USA) is true.

questions.stem:
The World Bank warned that India could become one of the first places where wet-bulb temperatures routinely exceed 35 °C. Which of the following statements best reflect(s) the implication of the above-said report?
I. Peninsular India will most likely suffer from flooding, tropical cyclones and droughts.
II. The survival of animals including humans will be affected as shedding of their body heat through perspiration becomes difficult.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation_md:
A wet-bulb temperature of **35 °C is the theoretical limit of human thermoregulation** — air so hot and humid that sweat cannot evaporate, so the body cannot shed metabolic heat and even a fit person in shade eventually dies.
- II — correct, and it is the direct implication: perspiration-based cooling fails for humans and other animals.
- I — accepted as correct: extreme wet-bulb readings are a heat-plus-humidity phenomenon concentrated in coastal, humid **Peninsular India**, and the same World Bank climate assessment projects the region facing intensified cyclones, flooding and droughts as part of the same warming.
Statement I is the weaker leg — cyclones and floods are consequences of the underlying warming the report describes, not of wet-bulb temperature as such — but the question asks what reflects the report's implications, and UPSC keyed both.
Worth remembering: wet-bulb temperature = heat **and** humidity combined; 35 °C wet-bulb, not 35 °C air temperature, is the survivability threshold.

independent_answer.reasoning: Wet-bulb 35 C implies bodies cannot shed heat via perspiration (II); flooding/cyclones/droughts (I) are not implications of wet-bulb temperature.

questions.review_flag: Official key says c, independent reasoning said b.

questions.stem: A country's fiscal deficit stands at ₹ 50,000 crores. It is receiving ₹ 10,000 crores through non-debt creating capital receipts. The country's interest liabilities are ₹ 1,500 crores. What is the gross primary deficit?
questions.explanation_md:
Gross primary deficit = gross fiscal deficit − interest payments = 50,000 − 1,500 = **₹48,500 crore**.
- The ₹10,000 crore of **non-debt creating capital receipts** (disinvestment proceeds, loan recoveries) is a distractor: those receipts are already netted out when the fiscal deficit itself is computed, so you do not subtract them again.
- (b) 51,500 adds interest instead of subtracting; (c) 58,500 wrongly adds back the capital receipts; (d) fails since (a) is exact.
Worth remembering: primary deficit strips **interest on past borrowing** out of the fiscal deficit — it shows how much of today's borrowing is for today's spending rather than for servicing yesterday's debt. Only interest payments move you from fiscal to primary deficit; nothing else in the question matters.

independent_answer.reasoning: Gross primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments = 50,000 - 1,500 = 48,500 crores; non-debt capital receipts are a distractor.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements with regard to recommendations of the 15th Finance Commission of India are correct?
I. It has recommended grants of ₹ 4,800 crores from the year 2022–23 to the year 2025–26 for incentivizing States to enhance educational outcomes.
II. 45% of the net proceeds of Union taxes are to be shared with States.
III. ₹ 45,000 crores are to be kept as performance-based incentive for all States for carrying out agricultural reforms.
IV. It reintroduced tax effort criteria to reward fiscal performance.

Consider the following statements in respect of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) :
I. It provides loans and guarantees to middle income countries.
II. It works single-handedly to help developing countries to reduce poverty.
III. It was established to help Europe rebuild after the World War II.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
The giveaway is "single-handedly" — the IBRD never works alone; it is one arm of the **World Bank Group**.
- I — correct: IBRD provides **loans and guarantees to middle-income countries** (and creditworthy low-income ones), raising funds on capital markets.
- II — incorrect: poverty reduction in the poorest countries is pursued jointly, above all with **IDA** (IBRD + IDA together constitute the World Bank), alongside IFC, MIGA and ICSID.
- III — correct: IBRD was created at **Bretton Woods in 1944** precisely to finance post-World War II reconstruction of Europe — its first loan went to France in 1947.
So I and III — option (c).
Worth remembering: "Reconstruction" in IBRD's name is the historical clue — Europe first, development lending later; IDA (1960) is the concessional window for the poorest, IBRD the market-rate window for middle-income borrowers.

independent_answer.reasoning: IBRD lends to middle-income/creditworthy countries and was created in 1944 to rebuild post-war Europe, but it works as part of the World Bank Group, not single-handedly.

Consider the following statements in respect of RTGS and NEFT :
I. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time to settle payments.
II. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
III. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Only the settlement-speed contrast survives scrutiny; the other two statements describe restrictions that RBI has since removed or that never existed.
- I — correct: RTGS settles each transaction **individually and in real time** (gross settlement); NEFT settles in **half-hourly batches** (deferred net settlement), so a short delay is inherent.
- II — incorrect: **inward transactions are free** in both RTGS and NEFT; charges, where levied at all, apply to outward remittances.
- III — incorrect: both systems now run **24x7x365** — NEFT since December 2019, RTGS since December 2020 — so neither has restricted operating days.
So I only — option (a).
Worth remembering: RTGS is for large-value transfers (minimum ₹2 lakh, no upper cap); NEFT has no minimum. Both are RBI-operated, unlike IMPS/UPI which ride on NPCI.
questions.tagging_note: No topic explicitly covers RBI payment systems (RTGS/NEFT); ECO-20 digital payments is the closest, ECO-04 banking structure secondary.

independent_answer.reasoning: RTGS settles in real time while NEFT settles in batches (I correct); inward transactions are free in both and both operate 24x7x365, so II and III are wrong.

- III New Zealand — yes: the realm adds Chatham Islands (UTC+12:45), Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau to the mainland zone.

- V Brazil — no: **exactly four** zones (UTC−2 to UTC−5), all contiguous territory.
So "only four" — option (b).
Worth remembering: "more than four" excludes Brazil precisely because four is not more than four — and France, with its overseas territories, holds the world record (twelve zones).

Consider the following statements :
I. Anadyr in Siberia and Nome in Alaska are a few kilometers from each other, but when people are waking up and getting set for breakfast in these cities, it would be different days.
II. When it is Monday in Anadyr, it is Tuesday in Nome.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
Anadyr and Nome sit on opposite sides of the **International Date Line**, so the calendar date differs even though they are geographically close — but the direction in Statement II is reversed.
- I — correct: Anadyr (Russia) keeps UTC+12 while Nome (Alaska) keeps UTC−9, a gap of about 21 hours; when either city is at breakfast time, the other is on a **different calendar day**.
- II — incorrect: the Asian side of the Date Line is **ahead**. When it is Monday in Anadyr, it is still Sunday in Nome; Nome reaches Monday only after Anadyr has moved into Tuesday — never "Tuesday in Nome while Monday in Anadyr".
So I only — option (a).
Worth remembering: west of the Date Line (Asia/Oceania side) is always the later date; crossing it eastwards you repeat a day, westwards you skip one.

independent_answer.reasoning: Across the date line Anadyr (UTC+12) is about 21 hours ahead of Nome (UTC-9), so simultaneous breakfasts fall on different days (I correct), but when it is Monday in Anadyr it is Sunday in Nome, not Tuesday (II wrong).

Consider the following statements with regard to pardoning power of the President of India :
I. The exercise of this power by the President can be subjected to limited judicial review.
II. The President can exercise this power without the advice of the Central Government.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation_md:
The pardoning power under Article 72 is judicially reviewable only on narrow grounds, and the President cannot exercise it independently of ministerial advice — so only Statement I holds.
- **I — correct.** In *Epuru Sudhakar* (2006), building on *Maru Ram* and *Kehar Singh*, the Supreme Court held the exercise of pardon is open to **limited judicial review** — mala fides, arbitrariness, non-application of mind, extraneous considerations.
- **II — incorrect.** *Maru Ram* (1980) and *Kehar Singh* (1988) settled that the President acts on the **aid and advice of the Council of Ministers** here as elsewhere; there is no personal discretion.

Remember: **Article 72** (President — covers death sentences, court martial, Union-law offences) vs **Article 161** (Governor — no court martial, and commuting is possible but pardon of a death sentence stays with the President).

independent_answer.reasoning: Pardoning power is subject to limited judicial review (Maru Ram, Epuru Sudhakar), but the President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers, so II is wrong.

The Constitution keeps the Speaker in office through a dissolution and lays down the removal procedure, but says nothing about resigning from a party — so I and III are correct.

independent_answer.reasoning: GAGAN provides additional accuracy/integrity and better air traffic management, but its benefits extend beyond aviation to rail, road, maritime and surveying, so III is wrong.
